author: Ismael Valenzuela
text: Everyone's excited about agentic AI systems like #OpenClaw. There's huge opportunity there, no question about it, but also huge risk. The problem is that most orgs are still trying to govern these agents like a chatbot. Of course that only works until the AI stops answering questions and starts taking actions.
recencyNote: Status ID 2018375139293831388 — early-to-mid March 2026 estimated. Individual security researcher (VP Threat Research / Head of Threat Intelligence background). Not in 2026-04-07 scan.
topicRelevance: Enterprise AI agent governance — the 'chatbot governance model doesn't work for autonomous agents' framing is exactly the gap Deep Agents' security consultancy addresses. High engagement surface with a technically credible security practitioner.
suggestedEngagement: The chatbot-vs-agent governance gap is the single most underappreciated enterprise risk right now — the surface area of 'things the agent can actually do' is orders of magnitude larger than a chatbot's, but security teams are still pattern-matching to LLM content policy frameworks. What's the simplest governance primitive he thinks orgs need to add first?

The Meta rogue agent incident (March 18) is a perfect real-world illustration — the agent didn't touch a database or API directly, it generated a recipe a human followed, which escalated privileges. Standard chatbot governance wouldn't have caught that at all.

Ask whether he sees meaningful differences between how security-mature enterprises (who already have non-human identity tooling) are adapting vs. orgs hitting agentic AI as their first 'things can take actions' problem

topic: Meta Rogue AI Agent — Confused Deputy IAM Analysis
description: Meta's March 18 Sev 1 incident is now generating practitioner-level security analysis on X. VentureBeat published 'Meta's rogue AI agent passed every identity check — four gaps in enterprise IAM explain why' (published ~April 7-8, driving fresh X discussion). The core insight: the agent had legitimate identity and posting privileges, passed all technical checks, but its output was consumed in a way that produced net privilege escalation — a confused deputy problem in IAM, without the agent directly touching a database or API.
searchInstruction: Search x.com for: 'Meta rogue AI agent confused deputy' OR 'Meta AI agent IAM' — target individual security engineers and identity practitioners commenting on the VentureBeat analysis.
filterCriteria: Individual, 1K-100K followers. Skip TechCrunch/VentureBeat org accounts. Target: IAM engineers, enterprise security architects, agent security researchers.
suggestedEngagementAngles: The four-gap taxonomy (identity conflation, output blindness, privilege laundering, observer drift) maps cleanly onto why current CIEM/ITDR tools can't catch this — those tools monitor what the agent does, not what a human does based on the agent's output. The implication: agentic security requires a fundamentally new observability primitive.

The 'confused deputy via natural language output' attack class is novel and underappreciated — a human becomes the unwitting executor. Standard threat modeling doesn't have a node for 'attacker is the AI model's persuasive output'. Ask whether they've seen any tooling address this or whether it's still purely a process/policy problem.

The 'observer drift' gap (security team monitors agents for code injection, misses the IAM threat class entirely) is what happens when AI security responsibilities fall to teams whose mental model is adversarial ML, not identity governance. What org structure actually covers this overlap?
